blurb: Rare blue-eyed pointed cat with white feet and a white inverted V on the face
description: The Snowshoe is a rare cat breed from the United States, a medium-sized short-haired pointed cat with blue eyes, white feet and an affectionate, social nature.
answer: The Snowshoe is a rare short-haired cat breed that originated in Philadelphia, United States, in the 1960s from Siamese and bicolor American Shorthair crosses. It is a medium-sized, athletic pointed cat with blue eyes and white feet, commonly described as affectionate and social.

body: In the 1960s a cat owned by Siamese breeder Dorothy Hinds-Daugherty in Philadelphia had three kittens with white feet. She bred seal point Siamese with bicolor American Shorthairs, then back to Siamese, and named the result Snowshoe. Vikki Olander later took over, wrote the first standard and won experimental status from the CFF and ACA in 1974. By 1977 she was the last US breeder, but others joined, and the breed gained CFF champion status in 1983, ACFA in 1990, TICA recognition in 1993 and full FIFe recognition in 2004. It is not recognized by the CFA.

The Snowshoe is a medium-sized cat of foreign type, combining the heft of the American Shorthair with Oriental length: long and firm, athletic rather than bulky. The head is a broad modified wedge with medium to medium-large ears and bright blue walnut-shaped eyes. The short, smooth, glossy coat has no noticeable undercoat. It is pointed, with all four feet white and, ideally, a white inverted V on the face. Kittens are born white and develop markings within one to three weeks, and the correct pattern is hard to breed, which partly explains the breed's rarity.

Snowshoes are commonly described as affectionate, sweet-tempered and mellow, social and devoted to their owners, and compatible with children and other pets. They are said to dislike being left alone for long periods and to cope better with another cat for company. They are described as intelligent, learning tricks such as fetch, and as enjoying water.
The coat changes seasonally and is reported not to need much grooming. Given their sociable nature, companionship and play suit them.

Conditions reported in the breed include urate urolithiasis (bladder stones), for which one review found the Snowshoe over-represented. Breed clubs recommend health screening of breeding stock and regular veterinary check-ups.

faq.q: Why is the Snowshoe cat rare?
faq.a: The breed's markings rely on genes that are hard to control, so few kittens match the standard's white feet and facial pattern.

faq.q: Are Snowshoe cats good with children?
faq.a: They are commonly described as social and compatible with children and other pets, though individuals vary.

faq.q: Do Snowshoe cats need much grooming?
faq.a: Their short, smooth coat with no noticeable undercoat is reported to need little grooming.
